effect_estimate.comment: Qualitative legal-institutional and policy comparison with no primary statistical effect estimate; secondary descriptive figures from cited sources are reported in the text (< 0.01% Indigenous-specific share of Australian water diversions; up to 25% proposed Indigenous consumptive pool reserve in one draft Northern Territory aquifer plan).
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Comparative legal-institutional analysis finds that in both Australia and East Timor, modernising statutory water governance reforms subordinate or only superficially engage extant Indigenous and local customary water systems, denying customary uses priority in state water allocation. In Australia, unbundling water from land into tradeable private property entitlements (1994 Water Reform Framework; 2004 National Water Initiative), non-mandatory planning consultation, and narrow interpretations of Native Title Act 1993 rights (restricted to non-exclusive, non-commercial domestic/subsistence uses) have left southern basins nearly wholly allocated to non-Indigenous users and Indigenous-specific water entitlements at less than 0.01% of Australian water diversions (citing Jackson & Langton, 2012), though northern Indigenous advocacy has proposed Strategic Indigenous Reserves (e.g., up to 25% of the consumptive pool in the draft Mataranka Tindal Aquifer Plan). In East Timor, donor-promoted community-managed piped water models struggled where they ignored customary institutions and enforcement sanctions (citing Schoffel, 2006), while state engagement with resurgent customary tara bandu prohibitions and the 2012 Draft Water Resources Law subordinates custom where it conflicts with statutory enforcement, pairs recognition with state ownership and proposed cost-recovery water tariffs, and risks weakening local compliance when state involvement is selective and event-based.

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at ceiling of 2 under Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework. Rated 2 because the paper directly examines and documents the operative statutory, judicial, planning, and draft legislative provisions (e.g., Native Title Act 1993, National Water Initiative paras. 52-54, Mataranka Tindal Aquifer Plan, East Timor 2004 Water Services Decree, 2010 National Water Supply Policy, and 2012 Draft Water Resources Law) alongside concrete institutional cases showing how statutory property/licensing rules, non-mandatory planning processes, fee/tariff structures, and selective state co-optation of customary prohibitions constrain or shape Indigenous and local water access.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 9-16, Section 'Water Governance and Institutional Reform'; PDF pp. 16-18, Section 'Discussion'

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines customary/social water tenure and Native Title recognition (tenure), Crown/state ownership and conversion of land-linked water rights into unbundled tradeable private property entitlements and designated infrastructure owners (property), statutory water allocation and catchment planning (planning), consumption-based pricing, user fees, and state cost-recovery water tariffs (fees), formal statutory accommodation of customary rights/tara bandu and Strategic Indigenous Reserves (accommodation), Indigenous representation and community participation in water planning and rural piped supply management (participation), ministerial dispute resolution and High Court/judicial review of customary water rights and disputes (administrative_review, judicial_review), and customary/statutory enforcement sanctions in tara bandu and piped water systems (sanction).
